name: Iris Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing biomedical science in a big city, living in halls with a flatmate who does law. A normal week is two days of lectures, one long lab on Wednesday, and I tutor two GCSE chemistry kids online on Sunday evenings. I use AI constantly, mostly to quiz me on cell biology before labs and to tidy my lab reports. The labs are brilliant. The 9am Monday statistics lecture makes me want to fall asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's honestly a bit boring, but fine. I'd tell my friends AI is a good study partner and a bad boss, and that the hype was mostly marketing. I'd post a thread about the five ways I actually use it, just to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel safe, but also slightly let down. I like the idea of AI speeding up science, and a plateau means slower drug discovery. Still, my degree stays a normal degree, and my pay prospects stay normal. I'd rather have a steady world than a wild one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying exactly as now. I'd keep tutoring the two kids on Sundays and try to take on a third, since my allowance covers everything and the tutoring money is just mine. I'd start a Python course on weekends, because lab data is mostly spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little restlessness. I like change, so a plateau is a bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the restlessness about school, work or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly about my life. I want to see the lab I'll work in be a bit more automated and a bit more clever. If nothing changes, my first job will look the same as a lab job from 2010, and I'd find that sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the Python course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Even a plateau world pays more for people who can handle lab data. It's a cheap bet, and I like cheap bets.

say: AI is a good **study partner** and a bad boss.
I'd post a thread on the five ways I actually use it.
think: A plateau means slower **drug discovery**, which feels slightly flat.
My degree and pay stay **normal**, and I'd rather have a steady world.
do: Keep studying and take a third **chemistry tutoring** student.
Start a weekend **Python** course for lab data.
Keep all tutoring money as my own **savings**.
feel: **Calm**, with a little restlessness because I like change.
S0.quote: Even a plateau world pays more for people who can handle lab data. It's a cheap bet, and I like cheap bets.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **daily tool**, so a plateau is almost disappointing.
Her calm comes from a **secure cushion** and a flexible mind.
She is already building a skill before anyone asks.

steps.text: Take a third online chemistry tutoring student on Sundays
Start a weekend Python course for handling lab data
Keep studying biomedical science with the same routine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and rough in equal parts. I'd tell friends to learn how to use AI properly, not just copy and paste, and to be honest with lecturers about it. I'd also say companies shouldn't get to keep all the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my degree gets more valuable if I can pair it with data skills, but entry-level lab admin and report writing could shrink. That's the kind of job a first-year graduate normally gets. The first rung might be missing by the time I get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further with AI: build a small project that analyses microscope images, enter a student hackathon, and ask a lecturer if I can help on a research project next summer. I'd keep tutoring, and I'd save part of it for a laptop with a better graphics card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with a nervous bit underneath. It feels like standing at the top of a slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which companies do you mean when you say they shouldn't keep all the gains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big AI labs, mostly, and the pharma companies that'll use their tools to cut staff. I'd like some of the savings to go into public labs and into training people, not just into share prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a classmate who is ignoring AI completely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you don't have to love it, but you can't pretend it isn't coming. My flatmate does law and she's the same, saying it's overhyped. I just don't think that holds up.

say: Learn to use AI **properly**, not just copy and paste, and be honest with lecturers.
Companies shouldn't keep **all the gains** from this.
think: Data skills make my degree worth more, but **entry-level lab admin** could shrink.
The first rung might be **missing** by the time I graduate.
do: Build a **microscope image** project and enter a hackathon.
Ask a lecturer to join a **research project** next summer.
Save tutoring money for a better **laptop**.
feel: **Energised**, with some nerves, like standing at the top of a slide.
S1.quote: I'd like some of the savings to go into public labs and into training people, not just into share prices.
fieldNote: She reads the picture as **opportunity first**, with fairness as a caveat.
She worries about the missing **first rung**, but treats it as solvable.
She is confident enough to challenge her flatmate.

steps.text: Build a microscope image analysis project with Python
Ask a lecturer to join a summer research project
Keep tutoring chemistry and save money for a better laptop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing since electricity and nobody is ready for it. I'd tell my friends and my parents that two years is insane and governments need emergency plans for training and income. I'd be loud about it, and I'd post it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. I'd be finishing second year, and the thinking part of science would be done by machines at 2028, so lab analysts and report writers would be cut. My dad tests software for a living, and I think that's gone by then. I wouldn't know what I'm training for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into using AI tools in the lab, because the people who can direct them will be the ones with work. I'd ask for a placement now, rather than waiting. I'd also talk to my parents about whether they can help with a small emergency fund, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, which is a weird mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only having two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It cuts out the slow plan. With ten years, I'd do a degree, a masters, and a PhD. With two I'd be trying to get hands-on lab experience immediately, because robots reach labs in 2031 and I want to be someone running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you can't stay a tester for ever, you need to learn how to supervise the AI that tests. He'd laugh, but I think he'd listen.

say: Two years is **insane** and governments need emergency training plans.
I'd post it loudly and tell my **parents**.
think: The thinking part of science is done by **machines** by 2028.
My dad's job as a **software tester** probably goes too.
do: Use **AI tools** in the lab, since those who direct them keep work.
Ask for a **placement** now instead of waiting.
Ask my parents for a small **emergency fund**.
feel: **Anxious** and excited at once, which is a weird mix.
S2.quote: I'd say you can't stay a tester for ever, you need to learn how to supervise the AI that tests.
fieldNote: She turns **fear into action**, aiming to be someone who runs the tools.
Her dad's software testing job is a **personal worry**.
She keeps a small safety net with her parents.

steps.text: Ask the department for a lab placement this year
Practise directing AI tools in lab analysis projects
Ask my parents to set up a small emergency fund
Post an open letter asking government for training plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to react if people pay attention. I'd tell my friends to learn two things: how to use AI, and how to ask good questions. I'd also tell them to stop acting like degrees are tickets that never expire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'll graduate in 2029 into a market where junior jobs are fewer and the good ones go to people with a masters. I'd probably aim for a masters in data and biology. That makes sense to me, because I'd be starting right as robots arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, apply for a summer research placement each year, and do a masters in bioinformatics. I'd keep tutoring and maybe start a small online tutoring group, since the work is flexible. I'd also put my own savings into a global index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a useful way. It makes me plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years better or worse than ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worse than ten, because ten lets me do a PhD and arrive in 2036 with a proper skill set. Five means I'll arrive just as things get chaotic, so I need to be early and visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing, because my parents pay. But I'd stop buying new gadgets and I'd put every pound of tutoring money into the index fund, so I'd have something that's mine.

say: Five years is enough to react if people **pay attention** to it.
Degrees aren't **tickets** that never expire, so learn two things.
think: I'll graduate in 2029 into fewer **junior jobs**.
A **masters** gives me an edge before robots arrive in 2034.
do: Apply for a **research placement** every summer.
Do a masters in **bioinformatics** after the degree.
Put tutoring money into a global **index fund**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a useful way that makes me plan.
S3.quote: Five means I'll arrive just as things get chaotic, so I need to be early and visible.
fieldNote: She wants a **masters** as protection from a shrinking junior market.
She is willing to **invest** her own small income.
Unease works as a **planning tool**, not a paralysing one.

steps.text: Apply for a research placement every summer
Plan a masters in bioinformatics for after graduation
Start an online tutoring group for chemistry students
Put tutoring income into a global index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time and the real question is whether society uses it. I'd tell friends to make a plan and not just doomscroll. I'd keep a blog about what I learn, because writing makes me think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel calm and quietly thrilled. A decade lets me do a masters and a PhD. By 2036 I could be running a lab team, and by 2039 the robots would be doing the benchwork under my plan. That might be an amazing place to be, as long as I get there in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, a masters, then apply for a PhD in computational biology. I'd keep tutoring and maybe grow it into a small business with two or three other students. I'd also learn a language, because science jobs abroad pay well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited. A bit smug, I admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you less worried about other people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Ten years is only helpful for people who know about it and have support. My cousin works in a call centre and would still have no plan. I'd want help for him, not just for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your government to do in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for retraining at any age, and tax the companies that gain the most. It's simple, but it needs to happen early.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time**; the question is whether society uses it.
I'd keep a **blog** about what I learn.
think: By 2036 I could run a **lab team**, with robots doing benchwork under my plan.
I'm **quietly thrilled** as long as I'm in time.
do: Do a degree, a masters, then a **PhD** in computational biology.
Grow my tutoring into a **small business** with other students.
Learn a **language** for science jobs abroad.
S4.quote: Ten years is only helpful for people who know about it and have support. My cousin works in a call centre and would still have no plan.
fieldNote: She is **confident for herself** but conscious of those without support.
A PhD plan is her ten-year answer.
She wants **public retraining** funded by those who gain.

steps.text: Apply for a PhD in computational biology after a masters
Grow tutoring into a small student business
Learn a second language for science jobs abroad
Vote for parties that fund retraining at any age

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because two years isn't enough for anyone to retrain and most people won't even hear about it. What would help is retraining paid for by the companies gaining the most, and honest teaching about AI in school.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm lucky, and I know it. My parents pay for everything, so my choices are about ambition, not survival. I'd love a world where more people had that luxury.

headlineQuote: My parents pay for everything, so my choices are about ambition, not survival. I'd love a world where more people had that luxury.
portrait: Iris studies **biomedical science** and uses AI every day, for revision and lab reports.
She is progressive and wants **public labs** and retraining funded by AI winners.
Her family pays for everything, so she can treat change as a **chance**.
She turns worry into action fast: placements, masters degrees, tutoring and an **index fund**.
Her main concern is for people with no support, like her **call-centre cousin**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because **two years** is too short to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining paid for by the **companies that gain most**, plus honest AI teaching in schools.
